meta.title: The Ma Files
meta.subtitle: How Jack Ma went from a business directory to the biggest IPO that never happened, and what changed when his companies started holding other people's money.
meta.disclaimer: General information for learning, not legal or financial advice. Rules differ by country and state; talk to a licensed attorney before you hold, move, or lend anyone's money.

ladder.oversight: Bank-style capital rules and the central bank

entries.title: An English teacher in Hangzhou
entries.summary: Born in Hangzhou, Ma failed China's college entrance exam twice, got in on the third try, and became an English teacher.
entries.body:
Ma Yun was born in Hangzhou in 1964. As a teenager he practised English by guiding foreign tourists around the city. He failed the national college entrance exam twice before passing on his third attempt and studying at Hangzhou Teachers College.

He graduated in 1988 and taught English there. In 1994 he opened his first business, a small translation agency. Nothing about this stage involved money belonging to anyone else, which is worth remembering for what came later.

entries.title: China Pages: a directory first
entries.summary: After seeing the internet on a 1995 trip to the US, Ma launched China Pages, an online directory of Chinese businesses.
entries.body:
On a 1995 trip to the United States, Ma searched the web and found almost nothing about Chinese companies. Back home he co-founded China Pages, one of the country's first internet businesses. It built web pages for Chinese firms and listed them so foreign buyers could find them.

China Pages faced a rival backed by the state telecom company, and Ma left within about two years. He then spent 1998 to 1999 building web projects for China's foreign trade ministry.

The important part for builders today: a directory sells visibility and information. It does not touch the payment between buyer and seller, so it sat outside financial regulation entirely.

entries.title: Alibaba starts in an apartment
entries.summary: Ma and a group of friends founded Alibaba as a business-to-business marketplace connecting Chinese suppliers with overseas buyers.
entries.body:
In 1999 Ma gathered roughly seventeen friends and colleagues in his Hangzhou apartment and founded Alibaba. The first site let manufacturers post products and buyers send enquiries: a richer, searchable version of the directory idea.

Alibaba took outside investment early, including money from Goldman Sachs and SoftBank. Those were private investors buying shares, the standard startup path, and they shaped the company's growth pace from the start.

entries.title: Taobao, then Alipay: the company starts holding the money
entries.summary: To make strangers trust each other online, Alibaba built Alipay, which held a buyer's payment until the goods arrived.
entries.body:
Alibaba launched Taobao in 2003 to compete with eBay in China. Strangers buying from strangers needed a way to trust each other, so Alibaba created Alipay: the buyer paid Alipay, Alipay held the funds, and the seller was paid once the buyer confirmed delivery.

That was escrow, and it is the hinge of this whole story. A directory or marketplace handles information. The moment a platform holds a buyer's money, it is doing something governments everywhere treat as finance. As smartphones spread, Alipay grew far beyond Taobao into paying for groceries, bills and everyday purchases.

details.Why it mattered: First time the business held customers' money

entries.title: Alibaba lists in New York
entries.summary: Alibaba's New York Stock Exchange listing raised about $25 billion, then the largest IPO ever.
entries.body:
Alibaba went public on the New York Stock Exchange in September 2014 and raised roughly $25 billion, a record at the time. Ma became China's richest person.

Alipay had already been moved into a separate, domestically controlled company in 2011 so it could hold a Chinese payment license. That business became Ant Financial, later Ant Group, and it was Ant, not Alibaba, at the centre of the 2020 collision.

details.Payments arm: Separated in 2011 for licensing; became Ant

entries.title: From payments to lending on thin capital
entries.summary: Ant built consumer and small-business lending where banks supplied most of the money and Ant supplied the data and the app.
entries.body:
Through products such as Huabei (a credit line) and Jiebei (cash loans), Ant let hundreds of millions of people borrow inside the Alipay app. Ant scored borrowers with its own data, but around a hundred partner banks provided most of the cash.

Ant's IPO prospectus showed it had facilitated about 1.7 trillion yuan of consumer loans and 400 billion yuan of small-business loans in the year to June 2020, with only about 2% of the consumer loans on its own balance sheet. Lending made up roughly a third of its revenue.

That structure let Ant grow lending enormously without the capital a bank would need. Regulators came to see it as a bank-sized risk sitting under tech-company rules.

entries.title: State-linked money joins Ant
entries.summary: Ant raised billions in equity, including from China's national pension fund, its sovereign wealth fund, state banks and state insurers.
entries.body:
In 2015 China's National Council for Social Security Fund bought a stake in Ant, reportedly at a discount. The 2016 round, about $4.5 billion at a $60 billion valuation, added China Investment Corporation, a China Construction Bank trust arm, China Life and China Post. A 2018 round of about $14 billion at roughly $150 billion brought in foreign funds such as GIC and Temasek.

These were equity investments: buying shares, not lending Ma money. Commentators at the time noted that state-backed shareholders could help with regulators. When the crackdown came, they did not stop it.

details.2016: CIC, CCB Trust, China Life, China Post (about $4.5B)

entries.title: The Bund Summit speech
entries.summary: Days before Ant's listing, Ma told a room of China's top financial officials that their rules were holding back innovation.
entries.body:
With Ant's IPO priced and the listing set for November 5, Ma spoke at the Bund Finance Summit in Shanghai. Senior regulators and bankers were in the audience.

He compared traditional banks' reliance on collateral to a pawnshop mindset, called the global Basel banking rules an old people's club, and argued that regulating fintech like banks would choke innovation. His argument directly concerned Ant's lending model. Nothing changed publicly that day.

entries.title: The biggest IPO in history, almost
entries.summary: Ant's dual listing in Shanghai and Hong Kong was set to raise about $34.4 billion, and retail investors bid around $3 trillion.
entries.body:
Ant planned to list on Shanghai's STAR Market and in Hong Kong at the same time, raising about $34.4 billion, more than Saudi Aramco's 2019 record. Reports valued Ant at more than $300 billion.

Demand was extraordinary. Retail bids came to roughly $3 trillion across both markets, and the Shanghai retail tranche was about 870 times oversubscribed.

entries.title: Summoned, and new lending rules the same day
entries.summary: Regulators met Ma and Ant's top executives, and draft online lending rules were published requiring lenders to fund 30% of joint loans.
entries.body:
On November 2, China's financial regulators held a meeting with Ma, Ant's executive chairman and its CEO. Reporting at the time said they were told the lending business would face much tighter oversight.

The same day, the central bank and banking regulator released draft rules for online microlending. Among them: a platform must fund at least 30% of any loan it makes jointly with banks, individual loans were capped at 300,000 yuan, and lenders needed far more registered capital. For a company funding about 2% of its loans, that rewrote the economics.

details.Meeting: Ma, Eric Jing, Simon Hu with regulators
details.Key draft rule: Fund at least 30% of jointly made loans

entries.title: The listing is suspended
entries.summary: Two days before trading, the Shanghai exchange suspended Ant's listing, and Hong Kong followed.
entries.body:
The Shanghai Stock Exchange suspended the listing, citing the regulatory meeting and changes in the fintech regulatory environment. Ant then halted the Hong Kong leg. Retail investors got their money back.

An IPO needs regulators' sign-off right up to the bell. The listing that was meant to be the finish line became the moment of maximum leverage for the people Ma had just criticised.

details.Halted by: Shanghai Stock Exchange, then Hong Kong
details.Stated reason: Regulatory meeting and changed fintech rules

entries.title: Ma disappears from view
entries.summary: Ma stopped appearing in public for about three months. There is no public evidence he was detained.
entries.body:
Ma skipped the final of Africa's Business Heroes, the TV competition he had created, and Alibaba cited a scheduling conflict. He did not appear in public for nearly three months, which set off worldwide speculation.

What is documented: no arrest, charge or detention was ever announced, and his companies did not say he was being prevented from appearing. A longtime Alibaba watcher told Reuters he believed Ma had been told to keep a low profile. Who told him, if anyone, has never been established. Everything beyond that is speculation.

entries.title: Alibaba's record antitrust fine
entries.summary: Regulators opened an antitrust case against Alibaba in December 2020 and fined it 18.23 billion yuan, about $2.8 billion, in April 2021.
entries.body:
In December 2020 China's market regulator opened an investigation into a practice merchants called choose one from two: sellers who also listed on rival platforms could be penalised with less traffic or fewer promotions.

In April 2021 Alibaba was fined 18.23 billion yuan, about $2.8 billion and about 4% of its 2019 domestic revenue, a record for China. It also had to file compliance reports for three years. In August 2024 the regulator said that rectification was complete.

This case was separate from Ant's lending problem. It is the risk that applies to any directory or marketplace that becomes dominant and tells sellers where they may or may not list.

entries.title: A 50-second video about rural teachers
entries.summary: Ma reappeared in a short video for his rural teachers programme and said nothing about the IPO, the regulators or his absence.
entries.body:
Ma resurfaced in a short online video for the annual ceremony of his foundation's Rural Teacher Initiative. He talked about education and poverty, and nothing about Ant, the regulators or where he had been.

It answered whether he was free. It did not answer why he vanished, and he has never publicly explained it.

entries.title: Ant becomes a regulated financial group
entries.summary: Ant agreed to reorganise as a financial holding company under central bank supervision, with bank-style capital rules.
entries.body:
In April 2021 Ant said it would apply to become a financial holding company so all of its financial businesses would sit under the central bank's supervision. That meant capital requirements closer to a bank's, and a valuation closer to a bank's too.

Investors had priced Ant as a fast-growing tech company. A supervised financial group with more capital tied up and more limits on growth is a very different business on paper.

entries.title: Ma gives up control of Ant
entries.summary: A shareholding overhaul cut Ma's voting power at Ant from more than 50% to about 6.2%.
entries.body:
Ma had controlled more than half of Ant's voting rights through holding entities. In January 2023 Ant announced that he and nine other key shareholders would vote independently instead of together, leaving Ma with about 6.2% of the votes and no single controlling shareholder.

Around the same time, a Hangzhou city government entity took a 10% stake in Ant's consumer finance unit as part of a capital raise. Ma kept his economic interest but lost the steering wheel of the company he founded.

entries.title: Ant fined, revamp declared finished
entries.summary: The central bank fined Ant about 7.1 billion yuan for governance and consumer-protection failures and for doing business reserved for banks and insurers.
entries.body:
In July 2023 the People's Bank of China announced a fine of about 7.1 billion yuan, roughly $984 million, and ordered Ant to shut down Xianghubao, its crowdfunded medical-aid product, and compensate users.

The stated violations included corporate governance, financial consumer protection, and taking part in business that should have been run by licensed banks and insurers. That last point is the clearest official statement of what went wrong: a tech platform doing finance without being regulated as finance.

details.Core violation: Doing bank and insurer business without being one

entries.title: Alibaba splits into six groups
entries.summary: Alibaba announced the largest restructuring in its history, dividing into six business groups, as competition from rivals grew.
entries.body:
In 2023 Alibaba divided itself into six main business groups, each initially allowed to explore its own fundraising or listing, and changed its top leadership. Rivals such as PDD and ByteDance's Douyin were taking e-commerce share.

Ma was no longer involved in day-to-day management. In 2024 he posted a rare long message inside Alibaba backing the restructuring and its new leaders.

entries.title: A quieter life, partly in Japan
entries.summary: Ma spent long stretches abroad and became a visiting professor at the University of Tokyo's Tokyo College.
entries.body:
Ma lived largely outside China for a period, including in Tokyo. From May 2023 he was a visiting professor at the University of Tokyo's Tokyo College, focused on sustainable agriculture, food production and entrepreneurship seminars.

Public speeches became rare. The founder who had sung to stadiums of employees and debated tech leaders on stage now appeared mostly in photos and short clips.

entries.title: Front row with Xi Jinping
entries.summary: Ma attended President Xi's symposium with private-sector leaders in Beijing, widely read as a sign the crackdown era was over.
entries.body:
In February 2025 Ma sat in the front row at a meeting Xi Jinping held with leading private entrepreneurs, alongside the heads of companies such as Huawei, Tencent, BYD, Xiaomi and DeepSeek. State television showed them shaking hands.

Analysts read it as Beijing courting private tech again while the economy slowed. Ant never revived the 2020 IPO, and Ma never returned to his old public role or explained the months he went missing.

entries.title: Holding money changes who your boss is
entries.summary: A directory or marketplace sells information. The moment you hold, move or lend customers' money, financial regulators get a say in how you operate.
entries.body:
China Pages and early Alibaba sold visibility. Alipay held buyers' funds, and Ant later steered trillions of yuan in loans. Every step across that line brought a new regulator with new powers: licenses, capital rules, consumer-protection duties and the ability to stop a listing.

Staying private does not keep you on the safe side. Ant was private when it built the lending business. The rules attach to the activity, not to whether you sold shares.

details.What happened to Ma: Ant was forced into bank-style supervision and fined for doing bank and insurer business
details.Your move: Keep funds flowing through a licensed processor so your platform never holds the money

entries.title: Lending with other people's capital draws a hard line
entries.summary: Ant facilitated huge loan volumes while funding about 2% itself. A single draft rule demanding 30% broke the model overnight.
entries.body:
Matching borrowers to lenders with your data is attractive because it scales without your own capital. It is also exactly the setup regulators worry about: the platform earns fees while banks carry the risk, and lending standards can slip.

If your plan involves financing, advances, buy-now-pay-later or revenue-based funding, assume rules can change to require you to keep real money at risk.

details.What happened to Ma: Draft rules required 30% funding on joint loans; the IPO was halted the next day
details.Your move: Refer customers to licensed lenders for a flat fee instead of sharing in loan risk

entries.title: Every investor buys a voice
entries.summary: Ant raised equity from state funds, banks and global investors. Each round added people with a stake in how the company behaved.
entries.body:
Ma did not borrow from the government. State-linked funds bought shares in Ant, alongside banks, insurers and foreign sovereign funds. That money accelerated growth and added stakeholders who expected a return and a smooth listing.

Slow, self-funded growth keeps decisions in your hands and avoids the pressure to reach a giant exit. It does not protect you from regulators, who act on what your business does rather than who owns it.

details.What happened to Ma: A long list of state-linked shareholders, and later loss of voting control
details.Your move: If you ever raise money, cap any one investor's say and never give up a veto over core decisions

entries.title: An IPO is a permission slip, not a finish line
entries.summary: A listing needs regulators' approval until the opening bell. Ant's was stopped two days before trading.
entries.body:
Going public means disclosing your model in detail, submitting to securities regulators, and asking permission at the moment you most need it. Ant's prospectus spelled out the 2% balance-sheet figure for everyone, including the officials writing new rules.

If you never plan to list, this risk mostly disappears. If you might, clean up anything a regulator could object to well before you file.

details.Risk level: Only if you plan to list
details.What happened to Ma: Record IPO suspended 2 days before trading
details.Your move: Grow without a listing deadline, and fix regulatory gaps long before any big raise

entries.title: Don't pick a public fight with the people approving your deal
entries.summary: Ma criticised regulators in front of them nine days before their sign-off mattered most.
entries.body:
Arguing for better rules is legitimate. Doing it on a stage, in front of the officials involved, days before they decide on your biggest transaction, turns a policy debate into a personal one. Reporting at the time said regulators took it that way.

The practical version for any founder: raise disagreements through comment periods, trade groups and private meetings, and keep public talk about your customers.

details.What happened to Ma: Speech on Oct 24; summoned Nov 2; listing halted Nov 3
details.Your move: Send rule complaints through formal comment periods, never a keynote

entries.title: Never make listings exclusive once you're big
entries.summary: Alibaba's record antitrust fine came from pressuring merchants not to sell on rival platforms.
entries.body:
A directory or marketplace becomes valuable when everyone lists there. The temptation is to protect that by punishing sellers who also list with competitors. Once you are dominant in your market, that is classic antitrust exposure in China, the US and Europe alike.

This risk applies even to a slow-growing, self-funded business. It turns on market share and behaviour, not on funding.

details.What happened to Ma: 18.23 billion yuan fine and three years of compliance reports
details.Your move: Win listings on value; never penalise businesses for listing elsewhere

entries.title: Data on everyone becomes something to supervise
entries.summary: Ant scored hundreds of millions of borrowers with payment data. Commentators argue that concentration of data alarmed Beijing as much as the lending did.
entries.body:
Ant's edge was knowing who paid whom, for what and how reliably. That made its credit scoring powerful and made the data itself a political concern. One of the source videos argues this was a central reason for the crackdown; that is commentary, not something officials stated.

The broader point holds anywhere: the more sensitive the data you collect, the more privacy, security and consumer-protection rules apply to you.

details.What happened to Ma: Credit scoring folded into regulated structures (official reasons focused on finance)
details.Your move: Collect the minimum, publish a plain privacy policy, and never sell user data

entries.title: Founder control can be unwound under pressure
entries.summary: Ma held over half of Ant's votes through holding entities and ended up with about 6.2%.
entries.body:
Layered holding structures can give a founder outsized control with a minority of the economics. Under regulatory pressure, Ant's major shareholders agreed to stop voting together, and that control evaporated without anyone buying Ma out.

Keep ownership simple and documented, so there is nothing for anyone to restructure in your absence.

details.What happened to Ma: Voting power fell from more than 50% to about 6.2% in Jan 2023
details.Your move: Hold direct, plainly documented ownership; avoid voting arrangements others can unwind

entries.title: The US version: money transmission and lending licenses
entries.summary: In the US, receiving money to pass on to someone else is generally money transmission, which needs a state license unless an exemption applies.
entries.body:
California's Money Transmission Act bars anyone from receiving money for transmission without a license or an exemption, and the state regulator (DFPI) enforces it. One exemption covers a platform acting as the payee's agent under a written contract, where paying the platform counts as paying the seller. Lending to Californians generally needs a California Financing Law license. Federally, money services businesses register with FinCEN.

The common safe pattern for directories and marketplaces is to never touch the funds: use a licensed payment processor that pays sellers directly, and take your fee from the processor's split.

This is general information, not legal advice. Have a fintech attorney confirm your setup before you launch any payment feature.

details.Common exemption: Agent of the payee, with a written contract
details.Your move: Route payments through a licensed processor and get an attorney's sign-off

entries.title: Slow organic growth: what it protects and what it doesn't
entries.summary: Self-funding keeps investors and IPO gatekeepers out of your decisions. It does nothing to exempt money handling, dominance or data from regulation.
entries.body:
Avoiding outside investors means no board pressure to grow into risky products, no cap table of strangers and no listing deadline. Those were real accelerants in Ma's story.

But the three problems that hit hardest (holding and lending money, exclusive deals with sellers, and control over sensitive data) would apply to a bootstrapped company doing the same things. Organic growth is a choice about ownership. Staying on the information side of the money line is a choice about activity. You need both.

details.Protects against: Investor control, IPO gatekeeping, growth-at-all-costs pressure
details.Does not protect against: Money rules, antitrust, data and consumer law
details.Your move: Write down which side of the money line each feature sits on before you build it

claims.claim: Ma criticised banks and regulators at the Bund Summit on Oct 24, 2020.
claims.note: Widely reported, including the pawnshop and Basel comments.

claims.claim: Regulators summoned Ma on Nov 2, 2020 and the listing was suspended on Nov 3.
claims.note: Confirmed by the Shanghai exchange statement and Reuters reporting.
The base raise was about $34.4 to $34.5 billion; $37 billion and higher figures include over-allotment options.
The fine was 18.23 billion yuan, about $2.8 billion. The narration mixed up the currency.

claims.claim: Ma's voting power fell from over 50% to about 6%.
claims.note: Reuters calculated 6.2% after the January 2023 overhaul.

claims.claim: Ma borrowed money from the government.
claims.note: State-linked funds bought equity in Ant (pension fund, sovereign fund, state banks and insurers). That is investment, not a loan.

claims.claim: Retail investors bid about $3 trillion for Ant shares.
claims.note: Reuters reported roughly $3 trillion in retail bids.

claims.claim: Ma was arrested or held under house arrest.
claims.note: No public evidence. No detention was ever announced.

claims.claim: By 2025 Ma was not permitted to speak for more than 30 seconds.
claims.note: No source found. Treat as the narrator's interpretation.

claims.claim: Ma's companies lost $891 billion in value by 2024.
claims.note: No source found for this exact figure.

claims.claim: The state took a golden share with veto power over Ant.
claims.note: Reports of state golden shares involved some Alibaba units, not confirmed for Ant itself. A Hangzhou government entity did take 10% of Ant's consumer finance arm.

claims.claim: A market-value chart showing Ant at $317B above JPMorgan.
claims.note: Not traced to a source; Ant's reported valuation was about $313B.

claims.claim: A photo of a shopkeeper in an Alipay shirt at a QR stand.
claims.note: Shows signs of AI generation (garbled Chinese characters). Not used here.
